textbookText: Chapter 10 Thermal Expansion William Thomson, also known as Lord Kelvin, was one of the most eminent scientists (a British physicist and mathematician) of the nineteenth century, and is best known today for inventing the international system of absolute temperature that bears his name. Thomson held a position as Professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of Glasgow.

Kelvin’s main achievements include the establishment of an absolute heat scale, publishing some studies on the systems of measurement units and patenting measuring devices such as the galvanometer, helping to perfect transmissions through submarine cables. He led to the establishment of absolute zero. Thomson also became the first scientist to serve in the House of Lords.

10.1 Introduction Thermal expansion is a fundamental concept in physics, which describes the change in size of a substance under the application of heat. When the temperature of a material increases under the application of heat, the atoms or molecules within the material begin to vibrate more, causing the average distance between them to increase. This results in the expansion of the material’s length, area and volume.
Thermal expansion is a phenomenon that affects a wide range of materials from solid s and liquids to gases. The degree of thermal expansion varies depending on the material’s

composition, molecular structure, and the strength of intermolecular forces. The water exhibits the unique behavior that it contracts as the temperature increases from 0C to 4C before expanding upon further heating.

The knowledge of thermal expansion is very crucial in the fields of engineering, architecture material science, etc. It plays a significant role in the designing and construction of structures, the development of precision instruments, and the study of thermal behavior of the materials. This chapter will explore the principles of thermal expansion, different types of thermal expansion, and their applications in various contexts.
